title: How to clean 925 silver jewellery at home safely
description: Clean 925 silver at home with a polishing cloth, mild soap or a foil and baking soda bath. Which method suits which piece, and what to never use on silver.
keywords: how to clean 925 silver jewellery at home
clean silver with baking soda and foil
intro: For light tarnish, a silver polishing cloth is all you need. For a dull or grimy piece, wash it in lukewarm water with a drop of mild dish soap and a soft toothbrush. For heavy tarnish on plain silver, a bath of hot water, baking soda and aluminium foil works well. The right method depends on how dark the piece is and what else is on it.

sections.heading: Before you start: check what you are cleaning
paragraphs: Turn the piece over and look closely. Three things change how you should clean it.
list: Stones: cubic zirconia is tough, but pearls, opals, turquoise, coral and glued-in stones do not like soaking or heat.
Plating: gold or rhodium plating is thin. Rubbing hard or using dips can wear it away.
Oxidised detailing: if the grooves are dark on purpose to show the design, aggressive cleaning will strip that look out.

sections.heading: Method 1: The polishing cloth (light tarnish)
paragraphs: A silver polishing cloth is a soft cloth treated with a gentle polishing compound. It is the safest tool for regular care and the one to reach for first.

Hold the piece flat on your palm and rub in straight, gentle strokes rather than circles, which can leave fine swirl marks. Use the treated side for tarnish and the plain side to buff. Do not wash the cloth, because that removes the compound. When it turns completely black and stops working, replace it. On gold-plated pieces, use only a plain soft cloth, since a polishing compound can wear the gold over time.

sections.heading: Method 2: Mild soap wash (dull, grimy pieces)
paragraphs: A lot of what looks like tarnish on a daily-wear pendant is actually soap, lotion and sweat residue. A simple wash clears it.

Fill a small bowl with lukewarm water and add one or two drops of a mild, plain dish soap. Soak the piece for five to ten minutes, then brush gently with a soft baby toothbrush, paying attention to the back of stone settings and the links of the chain. Rinse under running water with the sink plug closed, so nothing slips away. Pat dry with a soft towel and leave it to air-dry fully before you store it. Trapped water speeds up tarnish.

sections.heading: Method 3: Baking soda and foil bath (heavy tarnish on plain silver)
paragraphs: This method does not scrub tarnish off. It uses a chemical reaction between the silver sulphide and aluminium to turn the tarnish back towards silver, which is why it works on detailed pieces that are hard to polish by hand.

Line a heat-safe glass or ceramic bowl with aluminium foil, shiny side up. Place the silver on the foil so it touches it. Sprinkle about a tablespoon of baking soda per cup of water over the pieces, then pour in hot, just-boiled water. You may notice a faint eggy smell, which is the sulphur leaving. After a few minutes, lift the pieces out with a wooden or plastic spoon, rinse, dry and buff with a soft cloth.
Use this only on plain sterling or sterling with hard stones like CZ that are set with claws. Skip it for gold-plated pieces, oxidised designs, pearls, soft stones and anything with glue.

sections.heading: Things that do more harm than good
paragraphs: Home remedies travel fast on social media, but several of them are hard on silver.
list: Toothpaste: most are mildly abrasive and leave fine scratches, especially on polished surfaces and plating.
Bleach and chlorine cleaners: they can darken silver badly and damage stones.
Lemon with salt, or vinegar soaks for long periods: the acid and grit can etch the surface and hurt plating.
Paper tissue or kitchen towels for polishing: wood fibres can scratch.
Commercial liquid dips used on gold plated or oxidised pieces: they strip the finish along with the tarnish.

sections.heading: How often should you clean?
paragraphs: A quick wipe with a soft cloth after each wear goes a long way. A soap wash once every few weeks is enough for pieces worn daily. Save the foil bath for the occasional deep clean, not a weekly routine.

If you prefer pieces that need very little fuss, a rhodium or gold finish on sterling, like many of the [925 silver pendants](/silver) at Varaha, tarnishes less, as long as you clean it with only a soft cloth and mild soap.

faq.q: Can I clean silver with toothpaste?
faq.a: It is better not to. Most toothpastes are mildly abrasive and can scratch polished silver and wear through plating.

faq.q: Is the baking soda and foil method safe for silver?
faq.a: Yes for plain sterling and CZ pieces set with claws. Avoid it for gold-plated, oxidised, pearl or glued-stone jewellery.

faq.q: How do I clean a silver chain without tangling it?
faq.a: Soak it in mild soapy water, brush gently along its length while holding one end, rinse and lay it straight on a towel to dry.

faq.q: Can I wash silver jewellery with water?
faq.a: Yes, lukewarm water with a little mild soap is fine. The key is to dry it completely before storing.
